extracted.intended_audience: general readers, coin collectors (numismatists), and historians
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic Wikipedia article documenting the Monroe Doctrine Centennial half dollar: its specifications, history, design, production, distribution, critical reception, and numismatic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical and physical data for the coin: Value 50 cents (0.50 USD); Mass 12.5 g; Diameter 30.61 mm (1.20 in); Thickness 2.15 mm (0.08 in); Edge reeded; Composition 90.0% silver, 10.0% copper; Silver 0.36169 troy oz; Years of minting 1923; Mint marks S (all coins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exact measures and composition are the objective physical standards by which the issue is identified and compared to other U.S. coins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obverse and reverse designs (subject and designer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obverse: Conjoined heads of former presidents James Monroe and John Quincy Adams; Designer Chester Beach (design date 1923). Reverse: Stylized figures representing North and South America touch at the Panama Canal; Designer Chester Beach, resembling a design by Raphael Beck (design date 1923).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the iconography and credited artist(s); useful for attribution, cataloging, and assessing provenance or claims of resemblance to earlier works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design relief and detail (aesthetic and technical quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical assessments note the low/shallow relief which leaves the coin 'without sufficient detail' and gives a 'newly minted... insipid appearance'; portraits described as poor likenesses ('Adams, with his staring eye, is scarcely a portrait, and Monroe would not be recognized even by an expert').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low relief and lack of detail are cited as grounds for negative aesthetic judgments and affect collectors' perceptions of the design quality and desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design originality and plagiarism concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Raphael Beck complained that the reverse resembled his copyrighted 1901 Pan‑American Exposition seal; Beach faced accusations of plagiarism because of similarity to Beck's work. Correspondence and Commission of Fine Arts review followed; designers denied impropriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality and resemblance to earlier copyrighted designs are raised as evaluative criteria for artistic credit and controversy over design authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconography and symbolism (elements and intended meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse shows North and South America as draped figures touching at the Panama Canal, laurel (olive branch) for peace, Horn of Plenty, scroll and quill pen between dates 1823–1923 symbolizing the 'Treaty', faint lines representing ocean currents (Gulf Stream) possibly symbolizing trade routes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying iconographic elements and their symbolic interpretations is used to explain the design's intended message and historical references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical context and commemorative rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Issued in commemoration of the centennial of the Monroe Doctrine and produced as a fundraiser for the 1923 Los Angeles exposition tied to the motion picture industry; organizers associated the fair with the 100th anniversary to induce Congress to authorize a commemorative coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical association and the political/marketing rationale for issuing the coin are central to its interpretive significance and collector interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized mintage vs actual striking and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress authorized a mintage of 300,000 pieces; in May–June 1923, 274,077 were struck at the San Francisco Mint. Most were sent to the Los Angeles Clearing House; 77 pieces set aside for transmission to Philadelphia and the 1924 United States Assay Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorized mintage, actual struck numbers, and special set‑asides are important for rarity assessments and provenance tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales, release into circulation, and impact on survivor condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 27,000 half dollars were sold at $1; banks later released the remaining nine‑tenths of the mintage into circulation. Many pieces that had been saved were later spent during the Depression, so most surviving coins show evidence of wear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution decisions and subsequent release into circulation explain high rates of wear among surviving specimens and affect scarcity and market value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition/grading and market valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2015 Guide Book lists the coin at $75 in uncirculated MS‑60; an exceptional MS‑67 specimen sold for $29,900 in 2009. Many specimens have been treated to appear brighter; these, like other circulated pieces, are worth less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard coin grading (MS grades) and known auction results provide benchmarks for market value; altered or artificially treated pieces are devalued relative to genuinely uncirculated examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation/treatment and authentication considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted that many specimens have been treated to make them appear brighter or less worn; treated specimens are worth less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detecting treatment and distinguishing authentic uncirculated condition from artificial enhancement is a key criterion in valuation and authentication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception among numismatists and historians
rubrics_metrics.description: Diverse opinions recorded: some (Commission of Fine Arts' Moore) praised the model ('for sheer beauty equals this'), while other numismatists and art historians called the design 'uninspired', an 'aesthetic monstrosity', or 'insipid'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional and scholarly commentary informs collectors and historians about perceived artistic merit and contextual standing among U.S. commemoratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and special specimen handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventy‑seven pieces set aside for assay commission examination; some pieces were distributed to Philadelphia for testing; a small number were sold at premium at the fair and by mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provenance (where/when pieces were set aside, sold, or examined) can affect desirability and traceability of specific specimens.
